scientific_review_theme: Nonintersecting streamlines and velocity direction
teacher_note: In a well-defined nonzero steady velocity field, a location cannot have two different simultaneous velocity directions. At stagnation points the direction may be undefined; no general crossing is inferred. Source A remains best.

scientific_review_theme: Dye streak as a qualitative laminar indicator
teacher_note: A narrow, coherent dye streak along a smooth path supports ordered laminar motion in the intended demonstration. Dye injection, diffusion and local flow conditions affect appearance, so this is a diagnostic example rather than a proof for all flows.

scientific_review_theme: Abrupt geometry changes can disturb flow
teacher_note: A sudden tube bend or change in direction may promote separation and eddies in a suitable regime, but it does not force turbulence at every flow rate. Source D states may, so the original answer is defensible.

scientific_review_theme: Figure 6.6(a)/(b) exact textbook depiction
teacher_note: The prepared teacher master contrasts orderly streamline paths in panel (a) with swirling turbulent paths in panel (b), giving source B. Existing GitHub record references unit6-figure66; exact printed NBF Figure 6.6 panel order/caption at pp.95–96 was not directly reopened in this review. Teacher must confirm visual-source attribution before certified figure-based examination use.

scientific_review_theme: Tube-center faster only for appropriate laminar profile
teacher_note: The center moves faster than wall-adjacent fluid in a developed pressure-driven no-slip laminar pipe flow. Different laminar boundary and pressure-driving conditions need not produce this profile; steady means time-independent velocity at a position, not identical speeds across all positions. Original C remains intended.

scientific_review_theme: Critical speed depends on fluid and geometry
teacher_note: The transition threshold is flow-specific and Reynolds-dependent, not one universal speed; the source B explicitly recognizes this limitation and is scientifically correct.

scientific_review_theme: Eddies and increasing-flow transition
teacher_note: Emerging irregular swirls suggest transition toward turbulence as speed increases in the source scenario. A coherent vortex by itself is not sufficient to classify every flow as turbulent, so retain the stated irregularity context.

scientific_review_theme: Viscosity omitted in ideal fluid
teacher_note: Real fluids exhibit viscous momentum transfer and internal resistance; the ideal non-viscous model sets that effect aside while preserving density and pressure as potentially nonzero. A is supported.

scientific_review_theme: Incompressible does not require rest
teacher_note: The intended introductory incompressible assumption is unchanged density during motion and need not imply zero speed or pressure. Fluid mechanics can treat a material density field with additional nuance; D is valid within the stated model.

scientific_review_theme: Liquid compressibility is small not zero
teacher_note: For ordinary pressure variations, liquid density changes relatively little, making incompressibility a useful approximation; it does not assert literally zero real-liquid compressibility. D remains correct.

scientific_review_theme: Streamlined body drag benefit beyond exact B-35 definitions
teacher_note: Streamlining commonly reduces flow disturbance and can reduce form drag, but drag depends on body orientation, flow separation and Reynolds conditions. Original A is supported; however the official B-35 explicitly targets steady, incompressible and non-viscous IDEAL flow terms, so individual B-35 exam eligibility of this aerodynamic-design item needs teacher scope approval. B-42 is only a possible alternative candidate, not certified.

scientific_review_theme: Wind-tunnel aerodynamics and exact B-35 eligibility
teacher_note: Wind tunnels help engineers observe airflow and assess/improve aerodynamic design; source B is correct. This applied real-world aerodynamic-purpose question does not directly define steady, incompressible or non-viscous flow, so do not automatically certify it against B-35. Assess alternative official alignment separately.

scientific_review_theme: Dolphin information-box attribution and summative scope
teacher_note: A streamlined dolphin profile can reduce hydrodynamic resistance, so source A remains the best choice. The teacher-prepared master attributes the example to an NBF information box; the original printed pp.95–96 information-box wording/illustration has not been reopened. This is a supporting application not automatically a B-35 definition item; teacher approval needed for source attribution and official scope.

scientific_review_theme: Ideal model limitation
teacher_note: An ideal inviscid model neglects real shear dissipation and cannot capture every viscous or turbulent detail. Original C correctly identifies a limitation; no automatic blanket claim that all turbulence is absent in ideal mathematics is made.

scientific_review_theme: Incompressible density remains unchanged
teacher_note: Constant fluid density is the intended idealized incompressible characterization. Viscosity and steadiness are separate properties, so C correctly excludes claims that density constancy implies zero viscosity or zero speed.

scientific_review_theme: Honey-versus-water viscosity example outside B-35's core
teacher_note: Honey usually flows more reluctantly than water under comparable geometry, temperature and driving head due to higher dynamic viscosity; B is the source-best choice. The official B-35 targets ideal-flow steady/incompressible/inviscid definitions, whereas viscosity of real fluids is more directly related to B-41. Do not certify under B-35 without an individual cross-SLO review.

scientific_review_theme: Steady or laminar does not imply spatially uniform speed
teacher_note: Even for steady laminar flow, different fluid positions/layers can have different speeds. The forbidden claim is global identical speed everywhere; D is correct. Avoid presenting steady and laminar as universally interchangeable.

scientific_review_theme: Blunt obstruction promotes but need not guarantee eddies
teacher_note: An abrupt body can disturb flow and create a separated wake depending on conditions, not necessarily a turbulent wake at every Reynolds number. The question says often, making D the supported option.

scientific_review_theme: Non-viscous fluid can have nonzero density
teacher_note: Inviscid idealization excludes viscous shear stresses but does not require zero mass density or pressure. Density can remain nonzero, so original C is correct.

scientific_review_theme: Ideal-flow simplification pairs
teacher_note: The book-derived ideal-fluid model assumes incompressible and non-viscous behavior; this does not require zero mass, exactly equal velocities or absence of pressure. Original D best matches the model.
